messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cashier
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Hans Becker is a 76-year-old widowed man who came for treatment after months of insisting to himself that he ought to be able to manage on his own. He works part-time as a cashier in a neighborhood grocery store, a routine he took up after his wife died because he wanted structure and some contact with people. He had spent part of his youth as a civilian in a war zone in Europe, and although he had carried those memories quietly for decades, they returned with force in later life. What stays with him are not long coherent stories but stark visual fragments: a street blown open, shattered glass glittering in the air, the fixed look on a stranger’s face, the inside of a vehicle he had been trying to reach as shelling began nearby. At times he can describe these scenes in a flat, distant way, almost as if they happened to someone else. At other times an image seizes him so completely that he feels he is there again in the danger, not remembering but reliving.

Over the years Hans had come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that whatever trust he once had in other people, life, and God had worn away in that period. As these beliefs hardened, the old memories seemed to return with even more force. When he thought, as he often did, about why this had happened to him and what it had meant, he never arrived at comfort; instead he found himself staring again at those frozen pictures, convinced they proved what he already feared about the world. The memories in turn deepened the same conclusions. When a vivid image broke through, he was left certain afterward that nowhere is really safe and that something essential in him had been permanently damaged.

He speaks painfully about no longer being capable of the things that once defined him. Driving is the clearest example. He used to take pride in handling himself, in going where he pleased without relying on anyone. Now even riding in a car feels intolerable. The images tied to vehicles and sudden attack are so immediate that he avoids driving altogether and refuses lifts unless there is no other option. He has begun arranging his life around buses, short walks, and rides from a neighbor only when absolutely necessary. That restriction has made him feel older and diminished, and each new workaround seems to confirm his belief that he is not the man he used to be.

At the grocery store, these problems are woven into ordinary moments. Standing at his register, Hans watches customers closely, scanning faces, hands, tone of voice, any sign that someone might turn aggressive. If a man comes in tense or loud, Hans feels his body brace before he has consciously thought anything. He keeps himself on guard all day and has trouble settling even at night, lying awake because some part of him feels he must remain alert. When his guard is this high, the war memories come more easily; a customer’s expression, the slam of a cart, or the glimpse of a car through the front windows can pull up a visual flash so sharply that for a second he is not in the store but back in danger. And the more he lives in this state of watchfulness, the more convinced he becomes that his vigilance is justified, that people cannot be trusted and that the world will hurt you if you stop looking.

In response, Hans has narrowed his life further. He avoids cars, but he also pushes away positive feelings when they arise, because relief or pleasure feels unsafe, like letting his guard down. On better days he distrusts the lightness almost immediately. He also spends long stretches turning the trauma over in his mind, trying to understand why it happened and why it has followed him into old age. None of this brings peace. Pushing away good moments leaves him more fixed on danger, and all the searching for meaning seems only to circle him back to the same images and the same bleak conclusions. The less room he allows himself for ordinary ease, the more jumpy he becomes; the more he stays on edge, the more he feels the world has proven him right.

By the time he sought help, Hans was exhausted. Sleep had become fragmented by the felt need to stay alert, work was harder because he could not stop monitoring customers, and his dependence on others for transportation humiliated him. What finally brought him in was the fear that his life was shrinking to the size of his precautions. He said he was afraid that if this continued, he would spend whatever years he had left trapped between old pictures and constant watchfulness. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not happiness exactly, but the possibility of feeling safe enough to rest and to believe that he is still capable of living as himself.
